conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'no—not on current evidence' to the question of whether whole-body vibration therapy prevents fractures in osteoporosis sufferers, noting a paucity of direct evidence and stating that surrogate improvements in bone mineral density do not prove fracture prevention.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: no—not on current evidence.** Whole-body vibration (WBV) has not been shown reliably to *prevent fractures* in people with osteoporosis.

The strongest directly relevant evidence is a systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials in adults aged 50+ that evaluated falls, fractures, and bone outcomes. It was designed to assess fracture risk, but the available trial evidence was limited and does not establish that WBV lowers fracture incidence. Its population also was broader than people diagnosed with osteoporosis, so it cannot provide a firm osteoporosis-specific fracture-prevention conclusion.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6027066/

A review focused on women with osteoporosis reached the same essential point: there was a **paucity of research on direct fracture reduction**. It suggested WBV might improve balance or other neuromuscular risk factors for falls/fractures, but that is indirect evidence—not proof that fewer fractures occur.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6372741/

Some studies and meta-analyses report improvements or less decline in bone mineral density (BMD), particularly in postmenopausal women. But BMD is a surrogate outcome: an improvement in BMD alone does not demonstrate prevention of hip, vertebral, or other fragility fractures.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-022-06556-y

WBV therefore might be considered an adjunct exercise modality for selected people, particularly if it helps strength or balance, but it should not replace established fracture-risk assessment, osteoporosis medication when indicated, and conventional fall-prevention exercise. Current guidance emphasizes fall prevention alongside pharmacologic treatment and recommends moderate- to high-impact exercise (when safe) to reduce falls and bone loss.  
https://www.aafp.org/afp/2023/0700/practice-guidelines-osteoporosis-treatment
